topic.title: Histograms with unequal class widths (frequency density) and estimating the median
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One of the last three questions on M4 every series since Summer 2023 (Q21 to Q23), 6 to 14 marks in three to five parts: draw or complete, read, median or mean, then a stratified-sampling part on the same data. Examined again in M8.
mustMemorise: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width; area of bar = frequency
median: n ÷ 2, accumulate the bar areas to the class, then lower boundary + (needed ÷ class frequency) × class width
mean from a histogram: rebuild the table (frequency = density × width), midpoints, Σfx ÷ Σf
stratified share = group ÷ population × sample size, a whole number of people
notOnThisSpec: Frequency polygons (the phrase does not appear in the CCEA specification)
Open-ended classes: every CCEA class has two boundaries
Frequency density on the formula sheet (extended 2022-2023 sheet only; the page-2 Higher sheet has no statistics formulae)

note.title: Histograms with unequal class widths and the median from a histogram
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: frequency = frequency density × class width (the area of the bar)
estimated mean = Σ(frequency × midpoint) ÷ Σ frequency
stratified share = group size ÷ population × sample size, rounded to a whole person

notOnThisSpec: Frequency polygons: the phrase does not appear anywhere in the CCEA specification, so no bar-tops-joined polygon is ever asked for
Open-ended classes such as 60 < t: every CCEA class has two boundaries, so every bar has a width
Frequency density on the formula sheet: it was printed only on the temporary extended sheet of Summer 2022 and Summer 2023; the page-2 Higher sheet since 2024 has no statistics formulae
Histograms with equal widths and a Frequency axis are M1 bar-chart work (M1-HD strand), not this statement

mustBeAbleTo: Write a frequency-density row for every class of a table with unequal widths (frequency ÷ width) before drawing
Draw a histogram on a blank grid: linear scales chosen from the largest density, both axes labelled (Frequency density; the variable with its unit), bars touching at the class boundaries
Read a frequency back from a bar as its area (density × width), including part of a class assuming an even spread
Fix the vertical scale when the axis has no numbers, from the one bar whose frequency is given
Estimate the median: n ÷ 2, accumulate the frequencies to find the class, then move a proportional distance into it
Estimate the mean by rebuilding the frequency table (boundaries, widths, frequencies, midpoints) and using Σfx ÷ Σf
Compare two distributions with a sentence that uses both values (medians, or counts above a value)
Carry the class frequencies into a stratified-sampling part: group ÷ population × sample size, a whole number of people, with a line of reasoning
Work out a missing bar from a total, including the day's takings at a price for each class
sheet.howExamined: One question among the last three of the M4 paper (Q21 to Q23 of 22 to 24 questions), worth 6 to 14 marks in three to five parts, calculator allowed. Since Summer 2023 the parts run: complete or draw the histogram (2 to 4 marks), read frequencies or a count above a value (2 to 3), estimate the median (3 to 4) or the mean (4 to 6), then a stratified-sampling part that reuses the same frequencies (2 to 4). Some series print no numbers on the vertical axis and give one bar's frequency instead. The same statement is examined again in M8. Summer 2026 set a 7-mark missing bar worked out from a price for each class and the day's takings.
traps: Bars drawn to the frequencies rather than the densities: many candidates scored zero on the drawing (Summer 2025 M4 Q22(a))
An own scale that does not fit the grid, or a vertical axis without the label Frequency density, loses the scale-and-labels mark even with correct heights (Summer 2025 M4 Q22(a))

Median stops at naming the class or takes its midpoint; the proportional step inside the class was missing for the vast majority (Summer 2023 M4 Q21(b), Summer 2025 M4 Q22(b), November 2025 M4 Q23(b))

Unnumbered density axis not calibrated from the bar whose frequency is given, so nothing after it could be started (November 2025 M4 Q23(a)); reverse reading of a value with a count above it was all or nothing (Summer 2024 M4 Q21(b))
Mean attempted without rebuilding the table with correct boundaries and frequencies (November 2024 M4 Q21(c): only the most able finished)
Stratified part stops at the group count, or gives a decimal number of people; the majority scored zero (November 2024 M4 Q21(d), Summer 2025 M4 Q22(c), November 2025 M4 Q23(c))

workedExamples.stem:
The table shows the distances, $d$ km, cycled by 60 members of a cycling club on one Saturday.

| Distance ($d$ km) | $0 < d \le 10$ | $10 < d \le 25$ | $25 < d \le 35$ | $35 < d \le 55$ | $55 < d \le 75$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 8 | 24 | 15 | 10 | 3 |

On the grid, draw a histogram to illustrate this information. [4]

data.caption: A blank grid: 16 large squares across, 12 large squares up, no numbers printed.

steps.decision: The widths are not all equal, so the bar heights cannot be the frequencies. I write the widths down before touching the grid.

options: Because the height of each bar must be frequency divided by class width, so I need every width first
Because the widest class always gets the tallest bar
Because the widths tell me how many bars to draw
whyMenu.explain: With unequal widths the area of a bar, not its height, stands for the frequency, so every height is frequency ÷ width.

steps.decision: All five densities are worked out and written in a new row of the table before drawing anything. This row is where the first two marks live; in Summer 2025 most candidates who skipped it scored zero.

steps.working: Largest density is 1.6, so the vertical axis runs from 0 to 2 with one large square $= 0.2$. Horizontal axis: 0 to 80 km with one large square $= 5$ km.
steps.decision: I choose the vertical scale from the largest density, not from the largest frequency, and make sure the last class (75 km) fits on the grid.

options: So that the tallest bar uses most of the grid and the smallest bar (0.15) is still readable
So that the axis reaches 24, the largest frequency
So that every bar is the same width on the page
whyMenu.explain: The grid is scaled to the densities. A scale reaching 24 would squash every bar into the bottom of the grid and would show the marker that frequency was plotted.

steps.working: Label the vertical axis **Frequency density** and the horizontal axis **Distance, $d$ (km)**; number both scales.
steps.decision: The scale-and-labels mark is separate from the bars. An unlabelled vertical axis lost this mark in Summer 2025 even when the heights were right.
Each bar starts and ends exactly at its class boundaries. A gap between bars means the data is being treated as discrete, which it is not.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Histogram with bar heights 0.8, 1.6, 1.5, 0.5 and 0.15 (frequency density), vertical axis labelled Frequency density, horizontal axis labelled Distance, d (km), bars touching.

workedExamples.stem:
The histogram shows the times, $t$ seconds, taken by the swimmers at a gala to complete one length of the pool. The vertical axis has no numbers on it.

18 swimmers took between 40 and 50 seconds.

Calculate an estimate for the median time. [4]

options.caption: Histogram on a grid of large squares; the bars for 20-30, 30-40, 40-50, 50-70 and 70-100 seconds are 2, 5, 9, 5.5 and 1 large squares tall. The vertical axis is labelled Frequency density but carries no numbers.

steps.working: The $40 < t \le 50$ bar is 9 large squares tall and 1 large square wide, so its area is 9 large squares. 9 large squares $= 18$ swimmers, so one large square $= 2$ swimmers.
steps.decision: With no numbers on the vertical axis I calibrate from the one bar whose frequency I know. Area is what stands for frequency, so I count squares of area, not just height.

options: Because a bar's frequency is its area, so a known frequency fixes the value of one square of area
Because the tallest bar always has the largest frequency
whyMenu.explain: Frequency = frequency density × class width = area. Once one square of area is worth 2 swimmers, every other bar can be read by counting its squares.

steps.working: Areas in large squares: $2,\ 5,\ 9,\ 11,\ 3$. Frequencies: $4,\ 10,\ 18,\ 22,\ 6$. Total $n = 60$.
steps.decision: The $50 < t \le 70$ bar is 2 squares wide and 5.5 tall, so its area is 11, not 5.5. I rebuild the whole table before doing any statistics.

steps.working: Median position $= 60 \div 2 = 30$. Cumulative frequencies: $4,\ 14,\ 32,\ 54,\ 60$. The 30th value is in $40 < t \le 50$.
steps.decision: 14 swimmers are done by 40 s and 32 by 50 s, so the 30th lies inside this class. Naming the class is where most candidates stopped in Summer 2025; the next step is the one that separates the grades.

steps.working:
Values still needed inside the class: $30 - 14 = 16$ of its $18$. Fraction of the class width: $\dfrac{16}{18} \times 10 = 8.89$.

Median $\approx 40 + 8.89 = 48.9$ seconds.
steps.decision: I assume the 18 values are spread evenly across the 10-second class, move 16/18 of the way across it and add that to the lower boundary. The class midpoint, 45, would not earn this mark.

options: Because area stands for frequency, so passing 16 of the 18 values means passing 16/18 of the bar's width
Because 16 is the largest number in the working
Because the median is always closer to the upper boundary
whyMenu.explain: The bar is a rectangle, so its area grows in proportion to the distance across it; 16/18 of the values sit in the first 16/18 of the width.

twin.stem: Same gala, a second heat. The bar for $50 < t \le 70$ is now 7 large squares tall; every other bar is as before, and 18 swimmers still took between 40 and 50 seconds. Calculate an estimate for the median time. [4]

options.caption: Same grid; bar heights 2, 5, 9, 7 and 1 large squares.

workedExamples.stem:
The histogram shows the times, $t$ minutes, that 160 customers spent in a bookshop one Saturday.

(a) Calculate an estimate for the mean time spent in the shop. [5]

(b) A stratified sample of 32 of these customers is chosen for a survey. Work out how many customers who spent more than 20 minutes in the shop should be in the sample. [2]

options.caption: Histogram with the vertical axis numbered 0 to 8; bars over 0-5, 5-10, 10-20, 20-30 and 30-50 minutes at heights 4, 8, 5.5, 2.5 and 1.

steps.decision: First I turn the picture back into a table: frequency = frequency density × width for every bar. The total matching the 160 in the stem tells me the boundaries were read correctly. In November 2024 the candidates who skipped this table could not finish.
Each midpoint is halfway between the class boundaries. Upper boundaries would push every estimate too high.

options: Because I do not know the exact times, so each customer is represented by the middle of their class
Because the midpoint is always a whole number
Because the frequency density is measured at the midpoint
whyMenu.explain: The mean from grouped data is an estimate; the midpoint is the fairest single value for everyone in the class.

steps.decision: Frequency times midpoint for each class, then add. I keep the products visible so the method mark survives an arithmetic slip.
Divide by the total frequency, 160, not by the number of classes. The answer sits inside the data range and near the middle of the histogram, which is the sanity check.

steps.working: More than 20 minutes: $25 + 20 = 45$ customers. Share of the sample: $\dfrac{45}{160} \times 32 = 9$ customers.
steps.decision: A stratified sample keeps every group in the same proportion as the population. Finding 45 is only the first mark; the sample number is 45/160 of 32, and a count of people is rounded to a whole number if it does not come out exactly.

twin.stem: The following Saturday the bar for $30 < t \le 50$ has height 0.5 instead of 1; every other bar is unchanged. Calculate an estimate for the mean time spent in the shop. [5]

options.caption: Same axes; the last bar is now at height 0.5.

steps.decision: Start at the right-hand end, where the long eels are. The last bar lies wholly above 60, so all 12 count.
The next bar holds 1.5 × 10 = 15 eels, more than 9, so L lies inside that class.

options: Because the next bar holds more eels than are still needed
Because L is always in the middle class
Because the 50 to 60 bar is the tallest
whyMenu.explain: Adding whole bars from the right stops at the bar that would overshoot: 12 + 15 = 27 is more than 21, so L is inside the 50 to 60 class.

steps.decision: A count becomes a width when it is divided by the density: 9 eels at 1.5 for each centimetre take up 6 cm.
Step back 6 cm from the top of the class, because the long eels are at the top end.

items.stem: The class $20 < h \le 30$ has frequency 18. What is its frequency density?
items.skill: Calculate frequency density from a frequency and a class width

options.feedback: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width = 18 ÷ 10 = 1.8.
18 is the frequency. With unequal class widths the bar height must be 18 ÷ 10; drawing to the frequency scored nothing in Summer 2025 M4 Q22(a).
You multiplied by the width. Frequency density divides the frequency by the width of the class.
You divided the width by the frequency. It is the other way round: 18 ÷ 10.

items.stem: On a histogram the bars for $10 < x \le 15$ and $15 < x \le 35$ are the same height. The first bar represents 8 values. How many does the second represent?
items.skill: Read frequency as the area of a bar

options.feedback: Equal heights mean equal densities (8 ÷ 5 = 1.6). The second bar is 20 wide, so 1.6 × 20 = 32.
Equal heights mean equal frequency densities, not equal frequencies. The second bar is four times as wide, so it holds four times as many values.
20 is the width of the second class, not its frequency. Multiply the density 1.6 by that width.
You divided instead of multiplying. Frequency = density × width = 1.6 × 20.

items.stem: A histogram shows 50 values. The cumulative frequencies at the class boundaries are 9, 21, 38, 50. Which statement about the median is correct?
items.skill: Locate the median class and know the next step

options.text: It is in the third class, $\frac{25 - 21}{17}$ of the way across it
options.feedback: The 25th value is after 21 and before 38, so it is the 4th of the 17 values in the third class; move 4/17 of the way across that class.

options.text: It is in the third class, so it is the midpoint of that class
options.feedback: Naming the class is the first mark only. The median is 4/17 of the way across the class, not halfway; the Summer 2025 M4 report says most candidates stopped here.

options.text: It is the value halfway along the horizontal axis
options.feedback: The median splits the values (the area), not the axis. Use n ÷ 2 = 25 and the cumulative frequencies.

options.text: It is in the tallest bar
options.feedback: The tallest bar is the modal class (highest density). The median comes from cumulative frequency, which can put it in a different class.

items.stem: A bar covers $10 < t \le 25$ and its height on the frequency density axis is 2.4. What is its frequency?
items.skill: Read a frequency from a bar

options.feedback: Frequency = density × width = 2.4 × 15 = 36.
2.4 is the height, which is the density. The frequency is the area: 2.4 × 15.
15 is the class width. The frequency is the density multiplied by that width.
You divided the density by the width. Frequency is density × width.

items.stem: A histogram's vertical axis has no numbers. The bar for $30 < x \le 40$ is 6 large squares tall and represents 30 values. What is one large square worth on the vertical axis?
items.skill: Calibrate a frequency-density scale from one known bar

options.feedback: The bar's density is 30 ÷ 10 = 3, spread over 6 squares, so one square is 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5.
30 ÷ 6 ignores the width. The bar's density is 30 ÷ 10 = 3 first; then 3 ÷ 6 = 0.5 per square. November 2025 M4 Q23(a) was lost at exactly this step.
3 is the density of the whole bar, not of one square. Divide by the 6 squares of height.
30 is the frequency of the bar. A square on the vertical axis is worth a frequency density, found from 30 ÷ 10 ÷ 6.

items.stem: A school has 200 pupils, 60 of them in Year 10. A stratified sample of 40 pupils is chosen. How many Year 10 pupils should be in the sample?
items.skill: Proportional allocation in a stratified sample

options.feedback: 60 is the size of the year group in the school. Scale it to the sample: 60/200 × 40. November 2024 M4 Q21(d) was mostly lost by stopping here.
200 ÷ 40 = 5 is the sampling ratio (one in five). Apply it to the 60 pupils: 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
30% is the proportion, not a number of pupils. Take 30% of the sample size 40.

items.stem: You are asked to estimate the mean from a histogram. What is the first thing to write down?
items.skill: Order of operations for a mean from a histogram

options.text: A table with the class boundaries, widths, and frequency = density × width for every bar
options.feedback: Rebuild the table first; the November 2024 M4 report says candidates who did not could not put the calculation together.

options.text: The bar heights, ready to add and divide by the number of bars
options.feedback: Heights are densities, not frequencies, and dividing by the number of bars is not a mean of the data. Rebuild the frequency table first.

options.text: The upper boundary of each class, to multiply by its height
options.feedback: Midpoints represent the classes, and heights must be turned into frequencies before multiplying. Table first.
That is the start of the median. The mean needs frequencies and midpoints, so the table comes first.

items.stem: A stratified-sample calculation gives 7.7 people for one group. What goes on the answer line?
items.skill: Round a stratified allocation to a whole number

options.feedback: A count of people is a whole number; 7.7 rounds to 8. November 2025 M4 Q23(c) accepted the whole numbers either side of 17.1.
The method is complete but a decimal number of people loses the final mark.
There is no round-down rule; 7.7 is nearer 8. (Where the scheme allows either neighbour, 7 is also accepted, but the reason given here is not right.)
One significant figure is far too coarse for a count that is known to the nearest person; 8.

items.stem: The class $15 < x \le 35$ has frequency 26. What is its frequency density?
items.skill: Frequency density is frequency over width

options.feedback: 26 ÷ 20 = 1.3: frequency over the class width.
26 is the frequency. The height of the bar is 26 ÷ 20.
That is width ÷ frequency. Density is frequency ÷ width: 26 ÷ 20.
That multiplies by the width; density divides by it: 26 ÷ 20.

items.stem: A bar for $6 < t \le 10$ has height 4.5. What is its frequency?
items.skill: Frequency is the area of the bar

options.feedback: Height times width: 4.5 × 4 = 18.
4.5 is the density. The frequency is the area: 4.5 × 4.
That multiplies by the upper boundary, 10. The width is 10 − 6 = 4.

items.stem: 100 values have cumulative frequencies 22, 41, 73 and 100 at 10, 20, 30 and 50. The class $20 < x \le 30$ holds 32. Estimate the median.
items.skill: The median moves into its class

options.feedback: The 50th value: 41 are done by 20, so 9 of 32 are needed: 20 + 9/32 × 10 = 22.8.
25 is the middle of the median class; only 9 of its 32 values are needed.
30 is not the middle of the data; the median is the 50th value.

items.stem: On a histogram with no numbers up the side, a bar 2 squares wide and 6 squares tall stands for 48 values. What does one square of area stand for?
items.skill: An unnumbered axis is fixed by area

options.feedback: Area 2 × 6 = 12 squares; 48 ÷ 12 = 4 values a square.
48 ÷ 6 uses the height only. Count the bar's area: 12 squares.
48 ÷ 2 uses the width only. The bar's area is 2 × 6 = 12 squares.

items.stem: A histogram gives the frequencies 15, 25 and 10 for $0 < x \le 10$, $10 < x \le 20$ and $20 < x \le 40$. Estimate the mean.
items.skill: The mean from a rebuilt table

options.feedback: That uses the upper boundaries 10, 20 and 40. Each class stands at its midpoint.
750 was divided by the 3 classes. Divide by the 50 values.

items.stem: Of 120 values, 80 are greater than 20, and 24 of those are greater than 40. A stratified sample of 10 is taken from the values greater than 20. How many should be greater than 40?
items.skill: A sample from part of the data

options.feedback: 24/80 × 10 = 3: the population is the 80 values above 20.
24/120 × 10 uses all 120 values; the sample is drawn only from the 80 above 20.
24 is the group, not its share of the sample: 24/80 × 10.

context.setting: One class of a grouped table of parcel masses

parts.stem:
The class $10 < m \le 30$ has frequency 24.

Work out the frequency density of this class.
hints: Class width = 30 − 10 = 20.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
parts.workedSolution: Class width $= 30 - 10 = 20$. Frequency density $= 24 \div 20 = 1.2$.

commonErrors.feedback: You multiplied by the width. Frequency density divides the frequency by the class width: 24 ÷ 20.
24 is the frequency. The height of the bar is 24 ÷ 20 = 1.2.
You divided the width by the frequency. It is frequency ÷ width: 24 ÷ 20.

context.setting: A class with decimal boundaries (masses of eggs in grams, scaled)

parts.stem:
The class $2.5 < x \le 4$ has frequency 21.

Work out the frequency density of this class.
hints: Class width = 4 − 2.5 = 1.5.
parts.workedSolution: Width $= 4 - 2.5 = 1.5$. Frequency density $= 21 \div 1.5 = 14$.

commonErrors.feedback: You divided the width by the frequency. Frequency ÷ width: 21 ÷ 1.5 = 14.
You divided by the upper boundary 4 instead of by the width 1.5.

context.setting: Reading one bar of a histogram

parts.stem:
On a histogram the bar for $40 < x \le 65$ has height 3.2 on the frequency density axis.

Work out the frequency of this class.
hints: Frequency = frequency density × class width.
parts.workedSolution: Frequency $= 3.2 \times (65 - 40) = 3.2 \times 25 = 80$.

commonErrors.feedback: 3.2 is the height (density). The frequency is the area: 3.2 × 25 = 80.
You divided the width by the density. Frequency = density × width.

context.setting: Finding a class width from a bar

parts.stem:
A bar on a histogram has frequency density 7.5 and represents 45 values.

Work out the width of its class.
hints: Frequency = density × width, so width = frequency ÷ density.
parts.workedSolution: Width $= 45 \div 7.5 = 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: You multiplied. Rearrange frequency = density × width: width = 45 ÷ 7.5.

context.setting: Completing a frequency-density row before drawing

data.caption: Waiting times, w minutes, at a pharmacy counter.

parts.stem:
The table shows the waiting times, $w$ minutes, of 103 customers at a pharmacy counter.

Complete the frequency density row of the table.

scheme.for: at least two densities correct from 3, 4, 3.6, 1.5

hints: Divide each frequency by its width.

commonErrors.feedback: The frequencies were copied into the density row. Divide each by its class width: 3, 4, 3.6, 1.5.

context.setting: Part of one class, assuming an even spread

parts.stem:
The class $10 < x \le 20$ of a grouped table has frequency 35.

Estimate how many of these values are greater than 12.
hints: 12 to 20 is 8 of the 10 units of width.
Assume the 35 values are spread evenly across the class.
parts.workedSolution: Fraction of the class above 12: $\dfrac{20 - 12}{10} = 0.8$. Estimate: $0.8 \times 35 = 28$.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole class was counted. Only the part above 12, which is 8/10 of the width, belongs in the estimate.

context.setting: Total from a three-bar histogram

parts.stem:
The histogram shows the lengths, $l$ mm, of some seedlings.

Work out the total number of seedlings.
hints: Each frequency is height × width.
parts.workedSolution: $2 \times 10 + 3.5 \times 20 + 1.2 \times 20 = 20 + 70 + 24 = 114$ seedlings.

commonErrors.feedback: The three heights were added. Multiply each height by its class width first: 20, 70, 24.

context.setting: Calibrating a vertical axis with no numbers

parts.stem:
On a histogram the vertical axis is labelled Frequency density but has no numbers. The bar for $20 < x \le 30$ is 8 cm tall and represents 60 values.

Work out the frequency density represented by 1 cm on the vertical axis.

scheme.for: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 for the density of the known bar

hints: First find the true density of the known bar: 60 ÷ 10.
That density is spread over 8 cm of height.
parts.workedSolution: Density of the known bar $= 60 \div 10 = 6$. It is 8 cm tall, so $1$ cm represents $6 \div 8 = 0.75$.

commonErrors.feedback: 60 ÷ 8 ignores the width. The bar's density is 60 ÷ 10 = 6, and 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 per cm.

parts.stem:
The bar for $30 < x \le 50$ is 5 cm tall.

Work out the frequency of this class.
hints: Height 5 cm × 0.75 gives the density; then multiply by the width 20.
parts.workedSolution: Density $= 5 \times 0.75 = 3.75$. Frequency $= 3.75 \times 20 = 75$.

commonErrors.feedback: 3.75 is the density. Multiply by the width of 20 for the frequency.

context.setting: Median from a small grouped table

data.caption: Journey lengths, j km, of 30 delivery runs.

parts.stem:
The table shows the lengths, $j$ km, of 30 delivery runs.

Calculate an estimate for the median length.

scheme.for: 15th value; cumulative 3, 12, 24 so the median class is 10 < j ≤ 20

hints: 30 runs, so the median is the 15th value.
Cumulative frequencies 3, 12, 24: the 15th is in 10 < j ≤ 20.
3 of the 12 values in that class are needed: 3/12 of a width of 10.
parts.workedSolution: Median position $= 15$. Cumulative $3,\ 12,\ 24$, so the class is $10 < j \le 20$. Median $\approx 10 + \dfrac{15 - 12}{12} \times 10 = 12.5$ km.

commonErrors.feedback: 15 is the midpoint of the median class (and, by coincidence, the median position). Interpolate: 3 of the 12 values are needed, so 10 + 3/12 × 10 = 12.5.
20 is halfway along the axis, not halfway through the data. Use the 15th value and the cumulative frequencies.

context.setting: Median read from a labelled histogram

parts.stem:
The histogram shows the masses, $m$ kg, of the suitcases checked in at a small airport desk one morning.

Calculate an estimate for the median mass.

scheme.for: 20th value; cumulative 6, 18 so the median class is 15 < m ≤ 25

hints: Rebuild the table first: 0.6 × 10, 2.4 × 5, 1.8 × 10, 0.2 × 20.
40 suitcases, so the median is the 20th value.
Cumulative 6, 18: two more of the 18 values in 15 < m ≤ 25 are needed.
parts.workedSolution: Frequencies $6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 4$; $n = 40$; median is the 20th value. Cumulative $6,\ 18,\ 36$: the class is $15 < m \le 25$. Median $\approx 15 + \dfrac{2}{18} \times 10 = 16.1$ kg.

commonErrors.feedback: 20 is the midpoint of the median class. Only 2 of its 18 values are needed, so the median is just 2/18 of the way across: 16.1.
That is the middle of the tallest bar. The median is the 20th value by cumulative frequency, which is in the next class.
The heights were treated as frequencies (total 5). Multiply each by its width: 6, 12, 18, 4.

context.setting: Mean from a table with unequal widths

data.caption: Times, t minutes, spent by 30 visitors in an exhibition room.

parts.stem:
The table shows the times, $t$ minutes, that 30 visitors spent in one room of an exhibition.

Calculate an estimate for the mean time.
hints: Divide by 30.
parts.workedSolution: $\sum fx = 4 \times 5 + 10 \times 12.5 + 12 \times 20 + 4 \times 35 = 525$. Mean $\approx 525 \div 30 = 17.5$ minutes.

commonErrors.feedback: Upper boundaries were used. The midpoints are 5, 12.5, 20 and 35.
525 was divided by 4 classes instead of 30 visitors. A mean of 131 minutes is outside the data.
Rounding the mean to a whole number loses the accuracy mark; 17.5 is exact here.

context.setting: One stratum of a stratified sample

parts.stem:
A leisure centre has 150 members. 45 of them are in the $18 < a \le 30$ age group.

A stratified sample of 30 members is chosen. Work out how many members from this age group should be in the sample.
hints: The group is 45/150 of the members.
The same fraction of the sample of 30.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{45}{150} \times 30 = 9$ members.

commonErrors.feedback: 45 is the size of the group in the population. Scale it to the sample: 45/150 × 30 = 9.
150 ÷ 30 = 5 is the sampling ratio, not the answer. Divide the group of 45 by 5, or multiply 45/150 by 30.

context.setting: Stratified share that does not come out whole

parts.stem:
A choir has 240 members. 74 of them live in the town.

A stratified sample of 25 members is chosen. Work out how many members who live in the town should be in the sample.
hints: 74/240 of the sample of 25.
The answer is a number of people, so round to the nearest whole number.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{74}{240} \times 25 = 7.708\ldots \approx 8$ members.

commonErrors.feedback: The method is right; a count of people must be a whole number, so 8.
74 is the group size. Multiply 74/240 by the sample size 25.

context.setting: Two bars of equal height, different widths

parts.stem:
On a histogram the bars for $5 < x \le 8$ and $8 < x \le 20$ are the same height. The first bar represents 12 values.

Work out how many values the second bar represents.

scheme.for: density 12 ÷ 3 = 4, or widths in the ratio 3 : 12

hints: Equal heights mean equal frequency densities.
The second class is four times as wide.
parts.workedSolution: Density $= 12 \div 3 = 4$. Second bar: $4 \times 12 = 48$ values.

commonErrors.feedback: Equal heights do not mean equal frequencies. Frequency is area: the second bar is four times as wide, so it holds 48.
20 is the upper boundary of the second class, not its frequency. Use density × width: 4 × 12.

context.setting: A short histogram on a blank grid

data.caption: Heights, h cm, of 32 sunflower seedlings.
Blank grid, 12 large squares across and 8 up.

parts.stem:
The table shows the heights, $h$ cm, of 32 sunflower seedlings.

On the grid, draw a histogram to illustrate this information.

scheme.for: linear scales, vertical axis labelled Frequency density, horizontal axis in cm
three touching bars at the correct heights

hints: Widths 20, 10, 30.
Largest density 1.5, so a vertical scale to 2 fits.
parts.workedSolution: Densities $0.4,\ 1.5,\ 0.3$. Vertical axis 0 to 2 labelled Frequency density; bars over 0–20, 20–30, 30–60 at those heights, touching.

commonErrors.feedback: Bars at 8, 15 and 9 are frequencies. Divide by the widths: 0.4, 1.5, 0.3.
Heights right, label missing: write Frequency density on the vertical axis and number it evenly.

context.setting: Reverse reading: a count above an unknown value

parts.stem:
The histogram shows the times, $t$ minutes, that 80 callers waited for a helpline to answer.

20 callers waited longer than $T$ minutes. Estimate the value of $T$.

scheme.for: 10 callers above 40 minutes, so 10 more needed from 20 < t ≤ 40

hints: Start from the right: the 40 to 60 bar holds 0.5 × 20 = 10 callers.
10 more are needed from the 20 to 40 bar, at 1.5 callers per minute.
That is 6.67 minutes measured back from 40.
parts.workedSolution: Above 40: $0.5 \times 20 = 10$. Needed from $20 < t \le 40$: $20 - 10 = 10$ callers $= 10 \div 1.5 = 6.67$ minutes. $T = 40 - 6.67 = 33.3$ minutes.

commonErrors.feedback: That includes the whole 20 to 40 class (30 callers) plus 10, which is 40 callers, not 20. Only 10 of the 30 are needed.

context.setting: A survey of the lengths of 60 trout caught on a lough during one weekend

data.caption: The table shows the lengths, l cm, of 60 trout caught on a lough during one weekend.
Blank grid, 14 large squares across and 10 up, no numbers printed.

parts.stem: On the grid, draw a histogram to illustrate this information.

scheme.for: all five frequency densities correct: 0.5, 1.4, 3.2, 1.2, 0.35 (seen in a table row or as bar heights)
scheme.examinerNote: Bars drawn to the frequencies 5, 14, 16, 18, 7 earn nothing in this part.

scheme.for: linear scales that fit the grid and both axes labelled, vertical axis labelled Frequency density and horizontal axis in cm
five bars at the correct class boundaries with no gaps, heights to their densities

hints: The class widths are 10, 10, 5, 15 and 20, so the heights are not the frequencies.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. Start with 5 ÷ 10 and 14 ÷ 10.
The largest density is 3.2, so a vertical scale from 0 to 4 (one large square = 0.5) uses the grid well.
parts.workedSolution: Frequency densities: $5 \div 10 = 0.5$, $14 \div 10 = 1.4$, $16 \div 5 = 3.2$, $18 \div 15 = 1.2$, $7 \div 20 = 0.35$. Vertical axis 0 to 4 labelled *Frequency density*; horizontal axis 0 to 60 labelled *Length, l (cm)*. Bars over 0–10, 10–20, 20–25, 25–40 and 40–60 at those heights, touching.

commonErrors.feedback: The bars are drawn to the frequencies. With unequal widths the height must be frequency ÷ class width; the Summer 2025 M4 report describes this as the main reason for zero marks on the drawing.
Heights are right but the vertical axis has no label or an uneven scale, so the scale-and-labels mark is lost. Write Frequency density beside the axis and number it evenly.

parts.stem: Estimate the number of trout that were longer than 30 cm.

scheme.for: part of the 25 < l ≤ 40 class above 30 cm: (40 − 30) ÷ 15 × 18 = 12, or 12 seen

hints: 30 cm cuts the class 25 < l ≤ 40 two thirds of the way along.
Assume the 18 trout in that class are spread evenly, so 10/15 of them are above 30 cm.
Then add every trout in the 40 < l ≤ 60 class.
parts.workedSolution: Above 30 cm within $25 < l \le 40$: $\dfrac{10}{15} \times 18 = 12$. All 7 trout in $40 < l \le 60$ are longer than 30 cm. Estimate: $12 + 7 = 19$ trout.

commonErrors.feedback: You counted the whole of the 25 < l ≤ 40 class. Only the part above 30 cm belongs in the estimate: 10/15 of the 18 trout.
You added frequency densities. A count of trout is an area: density × width for each part of a bar.

parts.stem: Calculate an estimate for the median length of the trout.

scheme.for: cumulative frequencies 5, 19, 35 and the median class 20 < l ≤ 25 identified
(30 − 19) ÷ 16 × 5, or equivalent proportional step inside their class

scheme.examinerNote: 22.5, the class midpoint, earns the first two marks only.

hints: With 60 trout the median is the 30th value.
Cumulative frequencies: 5, 19, 35. The 30th value is in 20 < l ≤ 25.
You need 11 more of the 16 values in that class, so move 11/16 of the way across its width of 5.
parts.workedSolution: $n = 60$, so the median position is 30. Running totals reach $5$, then $5 + 14$, then $5 + 14 + 16 = 35$ by 25 cm, which places it in $20 < l \le 25$. Values still needed: $30 - (5 + 14) = 11$ of the 16 in the class. Median $\approx 20 + \dfrac{11}{16} \times 5 = 23.4$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: 22.5 is only the middle of the class you found. Eleven of its sixteen values are still needed, so the median lies 11/16 of the way across the class, not halfway.
30 is halfway along the axis, not halfway through the data. The median is the 30th of 60 values, found by adding bar areas.

parts.stem:
A stratified sample of 10 trout is to be chosen from those longer than 20 cm, to be tagged.

Estimate how many trout in this sample would have lengths between 25 cm and 40 cm.

Show your working out clearly.
hints: The population for this sample is only the trout longer than 20 cm: 16 + 18 + 7.
The 25 to 40 cm class is 18 of those 41.
Take 18/41 of the sample of 10 and round to a whole trout.

parts.stem:
The histogram shows the daily rainfall, $r$ mm, recorded at a weather station on every day of one autumn on which rain fell. The vertical axis has no numbers on it.

scale correct (1 per large square, or 2 days per large square of area)
frequencies from density × width (or squares × 2) for all five bars: 15, 30, 45, 40, 20

hints: You know one bar completely: 45 days over a width of 5 mm, so its frequency density is 9.
That bar is 9 large squares tall, so each large square on the vertical axis is worth 1.
Now frequency = density × width for every bar, and add.

Frequencies: $7.5 \times 2 = 15$, $10 \times 3 = 30$, $45$, $4 \times 10 = 40$, $2 \times 10 = 20$. Total $= 150$ days.

commonErrors.feedback: You added the bar heights as if each were a frequency. A frequency is an area: density × width for every bar.

parts.stem:

figures.alt: An incomplete histogram of canoe hire times over 0 to 8 hours: bars 0 to 1 at 10, 1 to 3 at 12 and 5 to 8 at 3, vertical axis Frequency density from 0 to 14; there is no bar over 3 to 5.

parts.stem:
The incomplete histogram shows the lengths of time, $t$ hours, for which canoes were hired one day.

Hire costs £8 for up to 1 hour, £14 for more than 1 hour up to 3 hours, £18 for more than 3 hours up to 5 hours and £25 for more than 5 hours up to 8 hours.

The takings for the day were £1037.

Work out the height of the missing bar for $3 < t \le 5$. Show your working out clearly.

scheme.for: frequencies 10, 24 and 9 from the bars (density × width)

hints: The bars you can see give their frequencies as areas.
Each class's takings are its hires times its price.
The missing class's takings give its hires; its width then gives the height.
parts.workedSolution: Frequencies: $10 \times 1 = 10$, $12 \times 2 = 24$, $3 \times 3 = 9$. Takings: $10 \times 8 + 24 \times 14 + 9 \times 25 = 641$ pounds. The missing class took $1037 - 641 = 396$ pounds, which is $396 \div 18 = 22$ hires. The class is 2 hours wide, so the bar's height is $22 \div 2 = 11$.

commonErrors.feedback: 22 is the number of hires in the class. The bar's height is its frequency density: 22 hires over a 2-hour class, so 11.

context.setting: Grouped data with unequal classes, the interquartile range estimated

parts.stem:
The table shows the lengths, $x$ mm, of 80 leaves.

| Length ($x$ mm) | $0 < x \le 10$ | $10 < x \le 20$ | $20 < x \le 40$ | $40 < x \le 60$ | $60 < x \le 100$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 12 | 20 | 30 | 16 | 2 |

Calculate an estimate for the interquartile range. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: the 20th and 60th values, in 10 < x ≤ 20 and 20 < x ≤ 40

hints: The quartiles are the 20th and the 60th of 80 values.
Find each one inside its class, the way you would find a median.
The interquartile range is the upper quartile minus the lower.
parts.workedSolution: Cumulative frequencies $12$, $32$, $62$, $78$, $80$. Lower quartile, the 20th: $10 + \tfrac{8}{20} \times 10 = 14$. Upper quartile, the 60th: $20 + \tfrac{28}{30} \times 20 = 38.7$. Interquartile range $\approx 38.7 - 14 = 24.7$ mm.

commonErrors.feedback: The quartile classes are right, but their midpoints, 15 and 30, are not the quartiles. Move the right fraction into each class: 14 and 38.7.

findTheMistake.stem: Cara is asked to draw a histogram for the cycling-club distances (frequencies 8, 24, 15, 10 and 3 in the classes 0–10, 10–25, 25–35, 35–55 and 55–75 km). Here is her plan before she draws.
studentWorking: Classes: 0–10, 10–25, 25–35, 35–55, 55–75, so the horizontal axis runs from 0 to 80 km.
Vertical axis labelled Frequency, scale 0 to 25 with one large square = 2.5.
Draw the five bars touching, each between its class boundaries.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The classes have different widths, so the heights cannot be the frequencies. Every height must be frequency ÷ class width, and the axis is then Frequency density, not Frequency. Line 3 inherits the error: the scale to 25 and the label Frequency both follow from it.
correction: Vertical axis labelled Frequency density, scale 0 to 2 with one large square = 0.2.
Draw the five bars touching at those heights.
findTheMistake.feedback: As written this scores 0 of 4: with no frequency densities there is no density mark, the scale-and-labels mark needs the label Frequency density, and the bars are at the wrong heights. The Summer 2025 M4 report says a lot of candidates scored zero on the drawing for exactly this reason, and that those who found the densities first usually went on to full marks.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairi is asked to calculate an estimate for the median mass of 48 parcels: 10 in $0 < m \le 2$ kg, 18 in $2 < m \le 5$, 14 in $5 < m \le 10$ and 6 in $10 < m \le 20$.
studentWorking: n = 48, so the median is the 24th parcel.
Cumulative frequencies 10, 28, 42, 48, so the 24th parcel is in 2 < m ≤ 5.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 replaces the median with the middle of its class. 10 parcels are done by 2 kg, so 14 more of the 18 in the class are needed; the median lies 14/18 of the way across the class, well above its middle.
correction: Values still needed: 24 − 10 = 14 of the 18 in the class.
findTheMistake.feedback: The 24th value and the class 2 < m ≤ 5 earn the first two marks. The midpoint earns nothing further: the third mark is for the proportional step 14/18 × 3 and the final accuracy mark follows it. Summer 2023 and Summer 2025 M4 reports both say most candidates gained the mark for the class and did not know what to do next; this step is the one that separates them.

findTheMistake.stem: From the bookshop histogram (frequencies 20, 40, 55, 25 and 20 customers in the classes 0–5, 5–10, 10–20, 20–30 and 30–50 minutes) Meabh is asked how many customers who spent more than 20 minutes should be in a stratified sample of 30 customers.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 45 is the size of the group in the population of 160, not its share of a sample of 30. A stratified sample keeps the same proportion, so the group's share is 45/160 of 30. A sample of 30 cannot contain 45 people, which the sanity check would have caught.
findTheMistake.feedback: Reading 45 from the histogram earns the first mark. The second mark is for scaling to the sample, 45/160 × 30, and the answer is then rounded to a whole customer. The November 2024 M4 report describes the majority scoring zero on the sampling parts, and the Summer 2025 report says candidates found the group counts and then stopped.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is asked to draw a histogram for the lengths of 40 worms: 6 in $0 < l \le 4$ cm, 10 in $4 < l \le 6$, 16 in $6 < l \le 10$ and 8 in $10 < l \le 16$. Here is her plan before she draws.
studentWorking: Classes 0–4, 4–6, 6–10, 10–16, so the horizontal axis runs from 0 to 16 cm.
Vertical axis labelled Frequency, from 0 to 16.
Draw the four bars touching, each between its class boundaries.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 uses the frequencies as the heights. The widths are 4, 2, 4 and 6, not equal, so each height must be frequency ÷ width; drawn as planned, the 6 to 10 class looks twice the 4 to 6 class when it holds only 1.6 times as many.
correction: Vertical axis labelled Frequency density, from 0 to 5
Draw the four bars touching at those heights
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 is right, and the bars touching on their boundaries would earn the bar mark if the heights were right. The first marks are for the densities, which line 2 skips, and the label must then be Frequency density.

findTheMistake.stem: From a histogram of 150 hire times (frequencies 24, 36, 45, 30 and 15 in the classes 0–10, 10–15, 15–25, 25–40 and 40–60 minutes), Odhran is asked how many hires longer than 25 minutes should be in a stratified sample of 40 hires.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 stops at the size of the group. A stratified sample keeps each group's share of the population: 45 of the 150 hires is the share to take of the 40 sampled, not the number to sample.
findTheMistake.feedback: Lines 1 to 3 are right and earn their mark. The sample number is the group's share: 45/150 × 40 = 12. A sample of 45 from a sample of 40 is the giveaway. The November 2024 report found most candidates scored nothing on this step.

prompts.prompt: On a histogram, what does the area of a bar represent?
prompts.answer: The frequency of that class (height × width = frequency density × class width).

prompts.prompt: The vertical axis of a histogram with unequal class widths must be labelled ____.
Steps to estimate the median from a histogram or grouped table.
prompts.answer: 1. n ÷ 2. 2. Add frequencies (bar areas) until the class containing the n/2-th value. 3. Values still needed = n/2 − cumulative frequency before the class. 4. Median ≈ lower boundary + (needed ÷ class frequency) × class width.

prompts.prompt: Two bars reach the same height but cover classes of different widths. Which holds more values?
prompts.answer: The wider one. Equal heights mean equal densities; frequency is area, so the frequencies are in the ratio of the widths.

prompts.prompt: The vertical axis has no numbers, but one bar's frequency is given. How do you fix the scale?
prompts.answer: Frequency ÷ width of that bar gives its density; divide by its height in squares to get the value of one square (or divide the frequency by the bar's area in squares to get the frequency per square). Then read every other bar by area.

prompts.prompt: Why is a median (or mean) found from a histogram only an estimate?
prompts.answer: The data is grouped: the exact value of each item is not known, so an even spread within each class (or the midpoint) is assumed.

prompts.prompt: Estimating the mean from a histogram: what comes before Σfx ÷ Σf?
prompts.answer: Rebuild the table: class boundaries, widths, frequency = density × width for every bar (check the total), then midpoints. Only then multiply, add and divide by the total frequency.

prompts.prompt: A population of N has g people in one group. How many of a stratified sample of n come from that group?
prompts.answer: g ÷ N × n, rounded to a whole number of people.

prompts.prompt: A stratified-sample share works out as 6.6 people. What is the final answer?
prompts.answer: 7 (a whole number). Leaving 6.6 loses the final mark; where the scheme allows either neighbour, 6 or 7 are both accepted, but never the decimal.

prompts.prompt: Is frequency density printed on the CCEA Higher formula sheet?
prompts.answer: No. The page-2 formula sheet has no statistics formulae (it was only on the temporary extended sheet of 2022-2023). Frequency density and the grouped mean must be recalled.

prompts.prompt: Class 3.5 < x ≤ 5 has frequency 27. Frequency density?
On a histogram, what does the area of a bar show?
Median inside its class: what fraction of the width do you move across?
prompts.answer: Values still needed ÷ the class frequency.

prompts.prompt: An axis with no numbers: what fixes the scale?
prompts.answer: The one bar whose frequency you are told.

prompts.prompt: Estimating a mean from a histogram: which value stands for each class?

findings.asked: Complete a frequency table from a histogram, draw the missing bar, then estimate the median.
findings.wentWrong: The table and bars were fine. For the median almost everyone earned only the mark for naming the class it lies in; the proportional step inside the class was not known.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Found n/2, subtracted the cumulative frequency before the median class, and took that fraction of the class width added to the lower boundary.
findings.rule: The median estimate is a position inside the median class, not the class itself.

findings.asked: Decide from a histogram whether a hospital's waiting-time target was met, with an explanation, then find the time above which a given number of patients waited.
findings.wentWrong: The target check went well, with follow-through where one frequency was misread. The reverse reading (a count above an unknown value) was all or nothing: candidates who did not start from the right-hand bars made no progress.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Added whole bars from the top end until the next bar would overshoot, then divided the values still needed by that bar's density to get the width to step back.
findings.rule: Work from the end of the histogram that the count refers to, and turn a count into a width by dividing by the density.

findings.asked: Read frequencies from a histogram, draw missing bars, estimate the mean, then use the histogram for sampling.
findings.wentWrong: Reading and drawing bars went well. Estimating the mean defeated most: midpoints or frequencies appeared but not a usable table with correct boundaries. The sampling parts were mostly scored at zero.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Rebuilt a frequency table (boundaries, midpoints, frequency = density x width) and then ran the standard estimated-mean method on it.
findings.rule: Convert the histogram back into a table before doing any statistics with it.

findings.asked: Draw a histogram from a table on a blank grid, estimate the median, then take a stratified sample.
findings.wentWrong: Many scored zero on the drawing because bar heights were frequencies, not frequency densities; others who had the densities lost marks on their own scale or on unlabelled axes. The median again stopped at the class. The stratified part separated the top candidates; many left it blank.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Computed frequency density for every class first, chose a scale that fitted the largest density, labelled the vertical axis, then used the class frequencies for the sample.
findings.rule: Height = frequency divided by class width; label the axis 'frequency density'.

findings.asked: Work out the frequency-density scale from one known bar, estimate the median, explain why it is an estimate, then use the frequencies for a stratified sample.
findings.wentWrong: Most could not fix the scale from the information given, so later parts collapsed; the median-in-class step was again missing. The 'why an estimate' mark was widely earned (data in groups, exact values unknown).
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Worked out what one small square represented (frequency 10 here), then read every bar's frequency from area.
findings.rule: Area of a bar equals its frequency; use a bar with a known frequency to calibrate the grid.

insight.ruleToRemember: Frequency = frequency density x class width, so a bar's area is its frequency. To estimate the median, find n/2, locate the class, and go a proportional distance into it. Always rebuild the table before finding a mean or a sample.
insight.aStarSignal: Chaining the whole thing: calibrate the density scale from one bar, rebuild the table, estimate the median within the class, then feed the class frequencies into a stratified sample - with each step labelled.
